svg.aria-label: Diagram: Cloud DNS private zones and visibility in Google Cloud; a private zone can only be queried by the VPC networks you authorize, and a zone with no authorized networks cannot be queried at all, with every query arriving through the metadata server at 169.254.169.254, and private zones supporting neither DNSSEC nor NS delegation; the VPC name resolution order runs an outbound server policy first, then response policies, then authorized private, forwarding and peering zones, then Compute Engine internal names, and only then the public internet, with GKE cluster-scoped resources checked before any of it; matching is by longest suffix, so a private zone takes over its whole subtree, and if the winning zone holds no matching record Cloud DNS returns NXDOMAIN rather than falling through to the public zone, demonstrated by the documented split-horizon example where two names exist publicly and only one is answered inside the VPC; overlapping rules allow a private zone to overlap any public zone and allow private zones in different VPC networks to overlap each other, while two private zones authorized for the same network may not share an origin unless one is a subdomain of the other; and ownership, where Shared VPC zones belong in the host project unless cross-project binding places them in a service project, limited to projects in the same organization
svg.title: Cloud DNS private zones: a private zone does not add names, it takes over a subtree
svg.text: A private zone does not add names to your VPC. It takes over a subtree of the namespace.
Everything under that suffix now answers from the zone, or does not answer at all.
Visibility is a list of VPC networks, and nothing else
“Only authorized networks are allowed to query your private zone; if you do not specify any
authorized networks, you cannot query the private zone at all.” A zone with an empty list is
created, billed, and unreachable.
Queries arrive only through the metadata server 169.254.169.254. No DNSSEC. No NS delegation.
There are no name servers to point anything at — which is what makes it private.
VPC name resolution order — the public internet is LAST
0. GKE CLUSTER SCOPE — cluster-scoped response policies, then cluster-scoped private zones.
“The cluster is the most specific scope, and Cloud DNS checks it first for a match.”
1. ALTERNATIVE NAME SERVER, if an outbound server policy exists — it supersedes everything below.
2. VPC-scoped RESPONSE POLICIES.
3. AUTHORIZED PRIVATE, FORWARDING and PEERING ZONES — by LONGEST SUFFIX. This is the step
that decides everything else on this page.
4. COMPUTE ENGINE INTERNAL zones.
5. PUBLIC DNS — follow the SOA record to publicly available zones. Only if nothing above matched.
The subtree takeover, in the documentation’s own worked example
“If the zone doesn’t contain a matching record, Cloud DNS returns NXDOMAIN.” There is no fallback
to the public zone. Winning the longest-suffix match ENDS the search.
Public zone gcp.example.com holds TWO records. The private zone of the same name holds ONE.
myrecord1 — from a VM: 10.128.1.35 | from the internet: 104.198.6.142
myrecord2 — from a VM: NXDOMAIN | from the internet: 104.198.7.145
Two names the world can resolve; one of them goes dark inside the VPC. Nothing is misconfigured.
THE RULE: a private zone must carry EVERY name under its suffix that your VMs still need.
What may overlap with what
• Public with public — NOT on the same name servers. Cloud DNS tries another shard, or fails.
• Private with public — always allowed. This is split horizon, and it is the point.
• Private with private, DIFFERENT networks — allowed. Same name, different answer per VPC.
• Private with private, SAME network — only if one is a subdomain of the other. Identical
origins on one network are refused, because longest-suffix matching could not choose.
Who owns the zone, when the network belongs to someone else
SHARED VPC, default: create the zone in the HOST PROJECT and add the Shared VPC networks to its
authorized list. #80’s split again — the network admin holds DNS too.
CROSS-PROJECT BINDING: create the zone in the SERVICE PROJECT and bind it to a network owned by
another project — so namespace ownership follows the application, not the network.
One hard boundary: the projects must be in the SAME ORGANIZATION. No cross-org binding.
GKE CLUSTER SCOPE narrows further: a zone visible to one cluster rather than the whole network.
Before you create a private zone for a name that already resolves publicly, inventory every name
under that suffix your workloads use. Each one you omit becomes NXDOMAIN the moment the zone
exists — with no error, no warning, and no indication that the zone is the cause.
